title: Polynomial Divisibility Construction
problem:
Problem:
Show that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that
$$
\frac{4^{n}+2^{n}+1}{n^{2}+n+1}
$$
is an integer.
solution:
Solution:
Let $f(n) = n^{2} + n + 1$. Note that
$$
f\left(n^{2}\right) = n^{4} + n^{2} + 1 = \left(n^{2} + n + 1\right)\left(n^{2} - n + 1\right)
$$
This means that $f(n) \mid f\left(n^{2}\right)$ for every positive integer $n$. By induction on $k$, one can easily see that $f(n) \mid f\left(n^{2^{k}}\right)$ for every positive integers $n$ and $k$. Note that the required condition is equivalent to $f(n) \mid f\left(2^{n}\right)$. From the discussion above, if there exists a positive integer $n$ so that $2^{n}$ can be written as $n^{2^{k}}$, for some positive integer $k$, then $f(n) \mid f\left(2^{n}\right)$. If we choose $n = 2^{2^{m}}$ and $k = 2^{m} - m$ for some positive integer $m$, then $2^{n} = n^{2^{k}}$ and since there are infinitely many positive integers of the form $n = 2^{2^{m}}$, we have the desired result.

title: Finite Möbius Iteration
problem: Given that $f(x) = \frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$, $f(0) \neq 0$, $f(f(0)) \neq 0$. Let $F(x) = \underbrace{f(\dots(f(x)\dots))}_{n \text{ times}}$. If $F(0) = 0$, show that $F(x) = x$ for all $x$ where the expression is defined.
solution:
Put $f^k(x) = \underbrace{f(\dots(f(x))\dots)}_{k \text{ times}}$. Then we have $f^k(x) = \frac{a_k x + b_k}{c_k x + d_k}$. From
$f^{k+1}(x) = f(f^k(x))$ we get:
$$
\begin{align*} 
a_{k+1} &= a a_k + b c_k \
b_{k+1} &= a b_k + b d_k \
c_{k+1} &= c a_k + d c_k \
d_{k+1} &= c b_k + d d_k 
\end{align*}
$$
But we also have $f^{k+1}(x) = f^k(f(x))$, so
$$
\begin{align*} 
a_{k+1} &= a a_k + c b_k \
b_{k+1} &= b a_k + d b_k \
c_{k+1} &= a c_k + c d_k \
d_{k+1} &= b c_k + d d_k 
\end{align*}
$$
Comparing, we get $b c_k = c b_k$ and $(a-d) b_k = b(a_k - d_k)$.
If $f^n(0) = 0$, then $b_n = 0$, so $b c_n = 0$. We are given that $f(0) \neq 0$, so $b \neq 0$. Hence $c_n = 0$. Also $b(a_n - d_n) = 0$ and hence $a_n = d_n$. Hence $f^n(x) = x$.

title: Symmetric Absolute Logarithms
problem: Given function $f(x) = |2 - \log_3 x|$, positive real numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy $a < b < c$ and $f(a) = 2f(b) = 2f(c)$. Find the value of $\frac{ac}{b}$.
solution:
Note that $f(x) = |\log_3(\frac{x}{9})|$ is monotonically decreasing on $(0, 9]$ and monotonically increasing on $[9, +\infty)$.
By the conditions satisfied by $a, b, c$, we know that $0 < a < b < 9 < c$ and
$$
\log_3\left(\frac{9}{a}\right) = 2\log_3\left(\frac{9}{b}\right) = 2\log_3\left(\frac{c}{9}\right).
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\log_3\left(\frac{ac}{b}\right) &= \log_3\left(9 \cdot \frac{a}{9} \cdot \frac{9}{b} \cdot \frac{c}{9}\right) \\
&= 2 - \log_3\left(\frac{9}{a}\right) + \log_3\left(\frac{9}{b}\right) + \log_3\left(\frac{c}{9}\right) \\
&= 2,
\end{aligned}
$$
namely, $\frac{ac}{b} = 3^2 = 9$.

title: Quadratic Logarithmic Equation
solution:
Solution:

Najprej uporabimo pravilo za logaritmiranje količnika:
$$(\log 1 - \log x) \cdot (\log 4 - \log x) = \frac{3}{4}(\log 4)^2.$$
Ker je $\log 1 = 0$, dobimo:
$$(-\log x) \cdot (\log 4 - \log x) = \frac{3}{4}(\log 4)^2.$$
Razpremo oklepaj:
$$-\log x \cdot \log 4 + (\log x)^2 = \frac{3}{4}(\log 4)^2.$$
Preuredimo enačbo:
$$(\log x)^2 - \log x \cdot \log 4 - \frac{3}{4}(\log 4)^2 = 0.$$
To je kvadratna enačba oblike $a^2 - ab - c = 0$ za $a = \log x$.

Izračunamo diskriminanto:
$$D = (\log 4)^2 - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}(\log 4)^2\right) = (\log 4)^2 + 3(\log 4)^2 = 4(\log 4)^2.$$

Rešitvi kvadratne enačbe sta:
$$\log x_{1,2} = \frac{\log 4 \pm 2\log 4}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\log 4 \pm \log 4.$$
Torej:
$$\log x_1 = \frac{1}{2}\log 4 + \log 4 = \frac{3}{2}\log 4 = \log 8,$$
$$\log x_2 = \frac{1}{2}\log 4 - \log 4 = -\frac{1}{2}\log 4 = \log \frac{1}{2}.$$

Iz teh rešitev dobimo:
$$x_1 = 8,$$
$$x_2 = \frac{1}{2}.$$

title: Rational Logarithmic Recurrence
problem: Consider a real number $a \ge 1$. The sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$ is given by $x_1 = a$ and $x_{n+1} = 1 + \log_2 x_n$, for any $n \in \mathbb{N}^*$. Determine values of $a$ such that all terms of the sequence are rational numbers.
solution:
For $a = 1$ or $a = 2$ we get the constant sequence $1$ or $2$ respectively.
We shall prove that these are the only values satisfying the problem.
To see this, let $x_n = \frac{k}{l}$ and $x_{n+1} = \frac{p}{q}$, with $k, l$ coprime positive integers, $p, q$ coprime positive integers with $q \ge 2$. Then
$$
\frac{k}{l} = x_n = 2^{x_{n+1}-1} = \sqrt[q]{2^{p-q}},
$$
implying $l^q 2^p = k^q 2^q$.
The last equality cannot be true, as the left hand side number has $2$ as factor at an exponent which is not divisible by $q$ ($p$ and $q$ are coprime), and the right hand side has the factor $2$ at an exponent divisible by $q$. So $q = 1$, thus $l = 1$, so, if all terms of the sequence would be rationals, they should be natural numbers.
As $2^n > n + 1$, for $n \ge 2, n \in \mathbb{N}$, we get $1 + \log_2 x < x$, for $x \in \mathbb{N}, x \ge 3$. As a conclusion, if all terms are positive integers and $x > 2$, an inductive argument shows that the sequence is decreasing, a contradiction. That is $a = x_1 \in \{1, 2\}$.

title: Coupled Logarithmic Equations
problem:
Problem:

Real numbers $x$ and $y$ satisfy the following equations:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x & = \log_{10}\left(10^{y-1}+1\right)-1 \\
y & = \log_{10}\left(10^{x}+1\right)-1
\end{aligned}
$$
Compute $10^{x-y}$.
solution:
Solution:

Taking 10 to the power of both sides in each equation, these equations become:
$$
\begin{aligned}
& 10^{x} = \left(10^{y-1} + 1\right) \cdot 10^{-1} \\
& 10^{y} = \left(10^{x} + 1\right) \cdot 10^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$
Let $a = 10^{x}$ and $b = 10^{y}$. Our equations become:
$$
\begin{aligned}
10a & = b/10 + 1 \\
10b & = a + 1
\end{aligned}
$$
and we are asked to compute $a / b$. Subtracting the equations gives
$$
10a - 10b = b/10 - a \Longrightarrow 11a = 101b/10
$$
giving an answer of $\frac{101}{110}$.

title: Three Exponential Sum
problem:
Problem:
How many real numbers $x$ are solutions to the following equation?
$$
2003^{x} + 2004^{x} = 2005^{x}
$$
solution:
Solution:
Rewrite the equation as $(2003 / 2005)^{x} + (2004 / 2005)^{x} = 1$. The left side is strictly decreasing in $x$, so there cannot be more than one solution. On the other hand, the left side equals $2 > 1$ when $x = 0$ and goes to $0$ when $x$ is very large, so it must equal $1$ somewhere in between. Therefore there is one solution.

title: Shifted Radical Equation
solution:
Multiply both numerator and denominator by the conjugate:
$$
\frac{\sqrt{2014+\sqrt{x}}}{2014-x} + \frac{\sqrt{2015+\sqrt{x+1}}}{2015-(x+1)} + \frac{\sqrt{2016+\sqrt{x+2}}}{2016-(x+2)} = \frac{\sqrt{2015-x+\sqrt{1}}}{(2015-x)-1} + \frac{\sqrt{2016-x+\sqrt{2}}}{(2016-x)-2} + \frac{\sqrt{2017-x+\sqrt{3}}}{(2017-x)-3}
$$
After multiplying by the common denominator we have:
$$
\sqrt{2014+\sqrt{x}} + \sqrt{2015+\sqrt{x+1}} + \sqrt{2016+\sqrt{x+2}} = 
\sqrt{2015-x} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2016-x} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2017-x} + \sqrt{3},
$$

1) $x=1$ is the solution of the equation:
$$
\sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{3} = \sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{3}.
$$

2) Denote $S = \sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{3}$. For $x > 1$ we have
$$
\sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{x+1} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{x+2} > 
\sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{3} = S.
$$
So the left-hand side is greater than $S$, and in the same way we analyze the right-hand side:
$$
\sqrt{2015-x} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2016-x} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2017-x} + \sqrt{3} < 
\sqrt{2014} + \sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2015} + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2016} + \sqrt{3} = S.
$$
So in this interval there are no roots. The same holds for $x < 1$.

title: Playground Attendance Equation
problem:
Yesterday in the playground the ratio of boys to girls was $3 : 2$. Today, the number of boys is the square of the number of girls and there are $6$ boys and $7$ girls less than yesterday. How many children were there in the playground yesterday?
(A) 12
(B) 13
(C) 15
(D) 25
(E) 30
solution: Yesterday there were $3t$ boys and $2t$ girls in the playground. Today, there are $3t-6$ boys and $2t-7$ girls. From $3t-6 = (2t-7)^2$ we get $4t^2-31t+55 = 0$, so $t_{1,2} = \frac{31\pm\sqrt{81}}{8}$. The only possible solution is $t = 5$, since $t$ is an integer. Yesterday there were $3t = 15$ boys and $2t = 10$ girls in the playground, or $25$ children altogether.

title: Deleted-Digit Difference
problem: Andriy wrote a 4-digit number. Olesya crossed out the last digit and it turned out that the difference between the initial number and the obtained number equals $2018$. Which number did Andriy write? Provide all possible answers.
solution:
Let $abcd$ denote the number Andriy wrote, then $\overline{abcd} - \overline{abc} = 2018$. Now we only need to pick corresponding digits. Obviously, $a = 2$ or $a = 3$.

With $a = 3$, $\overline{3bcd} - \overline{3bc} > 3000 - 399 > 2018$, hence, $a = 2$ and $\overline{2bcd} - \overline{2bc} = 2018$. Analogously, $b = 2$ or $b = 3$.

With $b = 3$, $\overline{33cd} - \overline{33c} > 3300 - 339 > 2018$, therefore, $b = 2$ and $\overline{22cd} - \overline{22c} = 2018$. Analogously, $c = 3$ or $c = 4$.

When $c = 4$, we get $\overline{224d} - \overline{224} > 2240 - 224 = 2016$, therefore, the first solution would be in the form: $2242 - 224 = 2018$.

When $c = 3$, we get $\overline{223d} - \overline{223} < 2239 - 223 = 2016$, which means previously found solution is unique possible.

title: Integer Sum and Product
problem:
Problem:

The sum of the product and the sum of two integers is $95$. The difference between the product and the sum of these integers is $59$. Find the integers.
solution:
Solution:

Let the two integers be $x$ and $y$.

Let $S = x + y$ (sum), $P = x y$ (product).

We are given:

$P + S = 95$  \quad (1)

$P - S = 59$  \quad (2)

Add (1) and (2):

$P + S + P - S = 95 + 59$

$2P = 154$

$P = 77$

Now substitute $P = 77$ into (1):

$77 + S = 95$

$S = 18$

So $x + y = 18$, $x y = 77$.

The integers are the roots of the equation:

$t^2 - (x + y)t + x y = 0$

$t^2 - 18 t + 77 = 0$

Solve for $t$:

$t = \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{18^2 - 4 \times 77}}{2}$

$= \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{324 - 308}}{2}$

$= \frac{18 \pm \sqrt{16}}{2}$

$= \frac{18 \pm 4}{2}$

So $t = \frac{18 + 4}{2} = 11$ or $t = \frac{18 - 4}{2} = 7$

Therefore, the integers are $7$ and $11$.

title: Shifted Sum-of-Squares Equation
problem:
Problem:

Find the real solution(s) to the equation $(x+y)^2 = (x+1)(y-1)$.
solution:
Solution:

Answer: $(-1,1)$

Set $p = x + 1$ and $q = y - 1$, then we get $(p + q)^2 = p q$, which simplifies to $p^2 + p q + q^2 = 0$. Then we have $\left(p + \frac{q}{2}\right)^2 + \frac{3 q^2}{4} = 0$, and so $p = q = 0$. Thus $(x, y) = (-1, 1)$.

title: Three-Speed Shuttle Meetings
problem:
Pedestrian, Cyclist and Motorcyclist start at 12.00 from town $A$ to town $B$ simultaneously. When each of them arrives at $B$ he whip rounds and moves to $A$, when he arrives at $A$ he again whip rounds and moves to $B$, and so on. After the start of the movement the first meeting is the meeting of Cyclist and Motorcyclist at some point $C$. By this time Pedestrian passes $1/6$ part of the distance between $A$ and $B$, and after 6 minute he meets Motorcyclist. The first meeting of Cyclist and Pedestrian is also held at $C$.
When do Pedestrian, Cyclist and Motorcyclist meet each other at the same point for the first time?
solution:
Answer: 13.30.
Let the distance between $A$ and $B$ be equal to $S$ (km), the speeds of Pedestrian, Cyclist and Motorcyclist be equal to $a$, $b$ and $c$ (km/h), respectively. By condition (the first meeting is the meeting of Cyclist and Motorcyclist), it follows that $a < b < c$. Let Pedestrian arrive at point $D$ at that moment when Cyclist and Motorcyclist meet at point $C$. By condition, $AD = \frac{S}{6}$. Then $\frac{AD}{a} = t_1 = \frac{S}{6a}$. Since $AC + (AB + BC) = 2S$ we have $t_1 = \frac{2S}{b+c}$. So, $\frac{S}{6a} = \frac{2S}{b+c}$, hence
$$
b+c=12a. \tag{1}
$$
From $t_1 b = \frac{Sb}{6a}$ it follows that $AC = \frac{Sb}{6a}$, so $CD = AC - AD = \frac{Sb}{6a} - \frac{S}{6} = \frac{S(b-a)}{6a}$. Therefore,
$$
\frac{S(b-a)}{6a} = \frac{(a+c)}{10}. \tag{2}
$$
By condition, to arrive at $C$ (the point of meeting with Cyclist) Pedestrian need the time $t_2 = \frac{AC}{a} = \frac{Sb}{6a^2}$. On the other hand, $t_2 = \frac{2S}{a+b}$, so $b(a+b) = 12a^2 \Leftrightarrow b^2 + ab - 12a^2 = 0 \Leftrightarrow (b+4a)(b-3a) = 0$. Since $b+4a > 0$ ($a$ and $b$ are positive), we have $b-3a = 0$, i.e. $b = 3a$. Now from (1) it follows $c = 9a$, and (2) gives $S = 3a$. Therefore, $AC = \frac{Sb}{6a} = \frac{3a \cdot 3a}{6a} = 1.5a$. It means that Pedestrian and Cyclist meet at point $C$ in $t_2$ hours after the start, $t_2 = \frac{1.5a}{a} = 1.5$. Moreover, for Motorcyclist we see $1.5 \cdot c = 13.5 \cdot a = 4 \cdot 3a + 1.5 \cdot a = 4S + 1.5a = AB + BA + AB + BA + AC$, which means that after 1.5 hours after the start he arrive at point $C$. Therefore, Pedestrian, Cyclist and Motorcyclist meet at point $C$ at 13.30.
